analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agents to get a judge's warrant before tapping state and local surveillance networks.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2026 with 7 Republican cosponsors and referred to two House committees; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The PRIVACY Act would stop federal law enforcement agencies from getting around warrant requirements by borrowing data collected by state and local police surveillance gear — license plate readers, surveillance cameras, long-range microphones, and similar devices. It would require a federal judge's warrant for that data, limit how long agencies can keep it, make improperly obtained data inadmissible in federal trials, and bar federal grant money from buying the listed surveillance devices, with several exceptions. It also adds public reporting, minimization rules, First Amendment protections, and a right to sue agencies that break the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people: anyone whose movements, vehicle, or conversations are captured by the growing network of local police surveillance cameras and license plate readers. It specifically protects defendants in federal court, who would learn about surveillance evidence through mandatory disclosure, and people exercising First Amendment rights, whom federal agencies could no longer track using this data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone tracked by police surveillance networks

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the head of a federal law enforcement agency to obtain a warrant from a federal judge before accessing, querying, or tasking any surveillance data collected by state or local police devices on the Attorney General's 'Jurisdictional Wall List,' which must include license plate readers, occupant-facing cameras, continuous-location cameras, and long-range microphones.

Data obtained without a warrant — or kept longer than the 30-day retention limit — could not be admitted as evidence in federal court, and the government must disclose it to the defense under Rule 16 and Brady obligations, closing a common gap where defendants never learn how they were found.

Federal funds, including Byrne JAG public-safety grants, could no longer be used to purchase or install the listed surveillance devices, subject to exceptions for toll collection, school-safety programs, case-bounded warrant-based use, and standard grants with minimization limits.

The bill bans using the data to track someone solely for exercising First Amendment rights, requires the Attorney General to publish semiannual reports with unclassified public summaries, waives sovereign immunity so individuals can sue for damages, and directs Inspectors General to audit compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies (FBI, DEA, ICE and others), which would lose the shortcut of pulling data from local surveillance networks without a warrant and would face new audits, reporting, and personal administrative sanctions for violations. Surveillance equipment vendors also pay: the pool of federal grant money they currently sell into would shrink.

drawbacks.text: The suppression and disclosure rules could slow federal investigations and, in some cases, allow guilty people to avoid conviction because warrantless-surveillance evidence cannot be used in federal court — the standard trade-off of any warrant requirement made explicit.

The funding ban on surveillance devices could take useful tools away from state and local police who rely on federal grants, such as license plate readers used to locate missing children or stolen vehicles, though the bill carves out exceptions for tolling, school safety, and warrant-based, case-specific deployments.

The bill regulates only federal use of the data; state and local police could still collect and keep the same surveillance, and purchase the same devices with their own money, so the underlying mass-collection apparatus would remain in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are real and well-constructed — warrant requirement, retention limits, disclosure to defendants, and a private right of action — but the bill is deliberately narrower than its name suggests: it does nothing to limit state and local surveillance itself, and its funding ban has enough exceptions that the device market shrinks rather than closes. The main cost is reduced investigative speed and, occasionally, evidence being suppressed, which is the intended price of the Fourth Amendment protections the bill says it is enforcing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-July 2026 and referred to both the House Judiciary and Oversight committees, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Keith Self introduced the bill on July 15, 2026, alongside Representatives Crane and Clyde, and it was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
Seven Republicans had signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats are listed.
The action history shows no further steps after the dual committee referral — no hearings, markups, or votes have been scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, the status quo persists: federal agencies keep accessing local surveillance data without federal warrants, and surveillance vendors keep selling devices into the grant-funded market. For now, the bill's absence has benefited federal law enforcement convenience and the surveillance industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and surveillance vendors, so far

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship is Republican — the sponsor, two original cosponsors, and 7 of 223 House Republicans total — with no Democratic cosponsors on record, though the bill has not drawn recorded opposition either.

industries.industry: Surveillance technology vendors (license plate readers, camera networks)
industries.note: These companies sell plate readers and camera networks largely into police markets, much of it funded by federal grants; Section 3 would bar federal funds, including Byrne JAG grants, from buying devices on the Jurisdictional Wall List. Their revenue comes from mass monitoring of ordinary people, which is what the bill's warrant rules would rein in.

Agencies that currently pull data from state and local surveillance networks without a federal warrant would need warrants, face 30-day retention limits, evidence suppression for violations, IG audits, and personal administrative sanctions. Their convenience and reach are what the bill restricts.

The bill explicitly preserves federal funding for toll-collection license plate systems on federal highways and for school violence-prevention programs, so those market segments are carved out of the ban and protected while other segments shrink.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsor growth, no hearing, and the bill sitting in two committees simultaneously — a structure that gives both chairs veto power — the most likely path is that it dies quietly at the end of this Congress. It could move faster only if a committee chair schedules it or attaches it to a broader package.
